feed.title: SHRINCS: an efficient hash-based signature scheme for Bitcoin (first draft)

entry.title: SHRINCS: an efficient hash-based signature scheme for Bitcoin (first draft)
entry.summary:
A comprehensive security analysis of SHRINCS has been made available through a public repository at [SHRINCS/Security-Analysis](https://github.com/SHRINCS/Security-Analysis). This repository comprises three distinct research papers. The main paper presents the complete specification of SHRINCS and delivers its EU-CMA security proof, with security being reduced to the properties of foundational cryptographic primitives such as tweakable hash functions, message-digest functions and pseudorandom functions (PRFs). The evaluation covers both classical and quantum adversarial models, providing concrete security bounds for each scenario.
Additional results are presented in two supplementary papers. One discusses a classical bound for interleaved target subset resilience (ITSR), which is a critical property for protecting the FORS scheme; this result extends beyond SHRINCS and applies to SPHINCS+ and SLH-DSA. The second paper addresses multi-target undetectability, establishing a quadratic quantum bound of 4q²/|M| that improves upon the previously known linear bound of 12q/√|M|. Both of these findings have broader implications for signature schemes beyond SHRINCS and are therefore documented separately.
The architecture of SHRINCS integrates a stateful component (FXMSS with WOTS+C) and a stateless fallback mechanism (SLH-DSA) under a single public key, utilizing a shared hash function across both paths. Due to this integration, security proofs cannot be treated as independent black boxes; instead, the formal proof framework unpacks and intertwines the component proofs, allowing reductions from one path to simulate aspects of the other. Furthermore, since the signer can select the structure of the stateful tree, the security guarantee must apply universally to all possible state configurations. The detailed specification is constructed through explicit game hops, each with precisely quantified loss, and every security bound is rigorously evaluated against the proposed parameter sets.
Significant discoveries emerged during the analysis process. One major observation concerns the cost of reduction: Previous work on SPHINCS+ established security bounds based on the forger’s running time, but the underlying reductions required building an entire virtual hypertree, which, at the FIPS 205 parameterization (h=63), involves more than 2^72 hash computations. Accounting for this computational effort yields a security margin of approximately 2^-52 for classical attackers. This issue was addressed by introducing a collection oracle, whose treatment is elaborated in Sections 4.3 and 5, leading to a revised formulation of the SPHINCS+ security bound.
Another key point relates to reprogramming, where both the stateful and stateless paths share a unique reprogramming step. The analysis provides a sharper bound for this step compared to generic approaches, resulting in an added security margin of 34 bits for the stateless path and 33.4 bits for the combined scheme. For the recommended parameters, the computed security bounds range between 121.4 and 122.7 bits for classical adversaries according to query-counting methodology, while for quantum adversaries the bounds correspond to 2^58.0 to 2^59.2 hash queries. These assessments rest on three conjectures: the validity of a specific SM-DSPR bound, the applicability of the collection-oracle lemma from idealized to practical hash functions, and the assumption that the WOTS+C signer’s counter search always completes successfully within 2^16 attempts.
The authors encourage broad participation in reviewing these drafts, noting the potential for errors given the complexity and size of the proofs. Feedback is welcomed via the [repository issues page](https://github.com/SHRINCS/Security-Analysis) or direct communication. Furthermore, there is ongoing work towards a Lean 4 formalization of the three documents, with progress tracked publicly at [this pull request](https://github.com/SHRINCS/Security-Analysis/pull/1). Peer review and community scrutiny are actively solicited to strengthen the overall reliability and confidence in the presented results.
